source_text: Quod autem multum ad distinctionem inter te et Manichaeum tenendam valere exi stimasti, ut diceres bonam quidem, sed primorum hominum tantum factam naturam, omnem autem deinceps per concupiscentiam fuisse subversam, etiam Manichaeus ita disseruit: Operae - inquit - pretium est advertere, quia prima anima, quae a Deo luminis manavit, accepit fabricam istam corporis, ut eam freno suo regeret. Venit mandatum, peccatum revixit, quod videbatur captivum, invenit articulos suos diabolus, materiam concupiscentiae in eam seduxit et per illam occidit. Lex quidem sancta, sed sancta sanctae, et mandatum et iustum et bonum, sed iustae et bonae. Sic etiam in illa ad Patricium epistula: Quasi de primae factum flore substantiae meliorem - dicit - secutis. Non ergo magnum est nec aliquid ad defensionem tui promovet, quod a criminatione naturae humanae Adam sequestrandum putasti, super cuius statu mox plenius disseremus. Hic monstrasse sufficiat nihil ita rude in tuis sensibus inveniri, ut non sit iam Manichaei volutatione detritum.
pass_a_gloss: But what you have estimated to avail much for holding a distinction between you and the Manichaean, that you would say a nature indeed good, but of the first humans only, made, but every thereafter through desire has been overthrown, the Manichaean also has discoursed thus: It is worth the work, he says, to advert, because the first soul, which flowed from the God of light, received this fabric of the body, that it might rule it by its bridle. The command came, sin revived, which seemed captive; the devil found his joints, seduced the matter of desire into it and through that killed. The law indeed holy, but holy of the holy, and the command both just and good, but of the just and good. So also in that letter to Patricius: As if made from the flower of the first substance better, he says, than those following. It is therefore not great nor does it promote anything to your defense, that you thought Adam must be sequestered from the accusation of human nature, over whose status we shall soon discourse more fully. Here it suffice to have shown that nothing so rude is found in your senses that it has not already been worn by the rolling of the Manichaean.

lemmas.lexica: Blaise Manichaeus; Julian's polemic label vs natural evil
LS concupiscentia=eager desire; Blaise Christian usage often sexual desire vs nuptiae
LS/Blaise natura=created constitution, not 'original sin' itself
LS peccatum=fault, error; Blaise Christian sin
LS lex; Blaise lex Dei / sacred Law

pass_b_english: You thought it would be highly effective in maintaining a distinction between you and Mani to say that nature was indeed made good, but only in the first humans, while afterward it was entirely overthrown through desire. Mani argued this way too: ‘It is worth observing that the first soul, which flowed from the God of light, received this structure of the body to govern it with its bridle. The commandment came; sin, which had seemed captive, came to life again. The devil found his own limbs, brought the material of desire into the soul by deception, and through it killed the soul. The law is indeed holy—but holy for a holy soul; and the commandment is just and good—but for a just and good soul’ (Romans 7:9–12) (compare Romans 7:9–12). Similarly in his letter to Patricius, he calls the first human ‘better than those who followed, as though made from the flower of the first substance.’

It is therefore no great thing, and contributes nothing to your defense, that you thought Adam should be excluded from the accusation against human nature. We shall soon discuss his condition more fully. Here it is enough to have shown that nothing in your ideas is so fresh that Mani has not already worn it out by rolling it over.

choices.why: Julian's standing charge: natural evil is Manichaean. Keep the sect-name, not 'dualists'.
Julian distinguishes nuptiae from concupiscentia; do not flatten to 'lust' as a nature-sin substance.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

bible_refs.note: Commandment arrives; sin revives, deceives, kills; law holy.
From Pass B Scripture tagging; wording follows Julian's Latin, not a modern Bible.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
